checkpoints: A single balance column is a number with no memory — it answers "how much" but never "why".
The moment a customer disputes a charge or an auditor asks which transfer moved the money, a single balance column gives you nothing.
Double-entry turns money into an append-only event log: each transfer inserts an immutable DEBIT and CREDIT pair.
The ledger is the source of truth, and account.balance is merely a cache you can rebuild anytime by replaying the log.
Auditability falls out for free: every movement is traceable and reconstructable.
The global invariant SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT) also falls out for free, proving no transfer ever created or destroyed money.
The cost of this approach is extra rows and writes.
The payoff is a ledger you can prove correct — non-negotiable in fintech.
2PC is correct on paper but lethal in production.
In phase 1, every participant enters a prepared state — locks held, write-ahead entry logged, but the write undecided — and waits for the coordinator's signal.

If the coordinator crashes right between phase 1 and phase 2, the participants are stuck prepared forever: the wallet's row locks stay held, nobody else may write, and the only exit is a human manually resolving that in-doubt transaction.
That is a liveness failure.
And funds locked mid-transfer violate any fintech SLA.
A saga inverts that trade: it sequences local transactions, pairs each forward step with a compensating action (the inverse business operation), and progresses optimistically with no global lock.
The price is weaker isolation — intermediate state may briefly be visible — but in return the system stays resumable and always live.
The essence here is not distributed atomicity but liveness plus convergence.

Writing balance updates directly with `UPDATE account SET balance = $1 WHERE id = $2` and no corresponding `ledger_entry` row bypasses the ledger entirely, breaking the double-entry invariant `SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)`.

Once the ledger and the cached `account.balance` diverge this way, the invariant check exposed at `GET /api/invariant` starts reporting a mismatch that has nothing to do with an underlying bug — the reconciliation "fix" itself is what caused it.

Without a `ledger_entry`, nothing distinguishes an automated system correction from a customer genuinely moving that money, so replaying the event log makes the correction look as if it never happened.
Without a `reconciliation_run` row, there is no way to answer when reconciliation last ran, what drift it found, or what it fixed — the audit history a proper reconcile loop is expected to persist.

The correct fix is a compensating `ledger_entry` shaped like a real transfer: the delta computed as a `BigInt`, direction set to `DEBIT` or `CREDIT` depending on sign, and a `compensating: TRUE` flag marking it as an automated correction rather than customer activity.
The compensating ledger entry insert and the `account.balance` update must happen together inside a single transaction (`BEGIN`/`COMMIT`), never as a bare `UPDATE` issued outside of any ledger write.
A `reconciliation_run` row should be inserted alongside the fix, capturing the trigger, the drift count, and the fixes applied, so each correction is traceable to a specific run.

The fix can be verified by calling `GET /api/invariant` and confirming `balanced: true`, and by querying `ledger_entry WHERE compensating = TRUE` to see the correction appear as a flagged, run-linked row rather than an untraceable balance edit.

The invariant endpoint runs two full-table `SUM(amount)` aggregations — one for DEBIT, one for CREDIT — over the entire `ledger_entry` table on every call, so its cost is O(rows) and grows without bound as the ledger grows.

`ledger_entry` is append-only and immutable: rows written yesterday never change, so re-summing the whole table from scratch on every 30-second poll re-derives an answer that was already correct before, wasting work on settled history instead of just accounting for new rows.

The correct fix is turning the aggregate from something RECOMPUTED on read into something MAINTAINED on write — a `ledger_summary` table (or a Postgres materialized view) that holds the running `totalDebits`/`totalCredits` and is updated the moment a transfer happens, rather than a blind cache slapped in front of the existing query.

The running totals can be updated inline, inside the exact same `BEGIN…COMMIT` transaction that already inserts the debit/credit `ledger_entry` rows, so the summary can never drift out of sync with what was actually written — or updated asynchronously through a CDC stream, such as Debezium tailing the Postgres WAL, feeding a small consumer that applies each new row to the summary.

If a materialized view is used instead of a hand-maintained summary table, it needs a periodic job — for example a NestJS `@Cron()` task — to run `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` so the view stays reasonably current.

After the fix, `GET /invariant` becomes a single-row read like `SELECT totalDebits, totalCredits FROM ledger_summary`, which is O(1) regardless of whether `ledger_entry` holds thousands or billions of rows.

`account.balance` is already an example of this exact write-through-cache pattern, updated inline with every transfer, which is why per-account balance reads are already O(1); only the global invariant check was still doing the expensive full recompute.

Moving to an incrementally maintained total introduces a new risk — a bug in the increment logic or CDC consumer could silently drift from the truth — so a periodic authoritative full-table SUM, such as a nightly reconciliation job, must still run and alert loudly the moment it diverges from the cached totals, keeping the cheap O(1) check honest without paying its cost on every poll.

A nightly full scan that walks every account regardless of recent activity is bound by two independent constraints at once — the total account count and a single concurrency=1 worker draining the queue serially — so once the account base reaches billions, no amount of per-query speedup removes that ceiling; the bottleneck is architectural, not a slow SUM query.

Partitioning the account base (by id hash, by country, or by product line) into separate queues, each with its own worker, turns one serial walk over the entire dataset into many partitions reconciling in parallel, directly addressing the throughput ceiling.

An activity-driven filter — a CDC stream off the ledger table (e.g. Debezium), or a lighter mechanism like Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY — lets a run skip accounts with no new activity since the last cut-off, instead of recomputing the ledger SUM for every account whether or not it changed since yesterday.

Partitioning and activity-driven filtering solve two different kinds of waste and are complementary rather than substitutes for each other: partitioning alone still re-sums every untouched account inside each partition, while filtering alone still funnels every matching account through a single worker per partition.

Keeping each partition's queue at concurrency=1 preserves the original safety property that no two workers can ever race on the same account and post two separate compensating entries for the same drift.

Reconciling against a single cut-off timestamp captured once at the start of a run, rather than an open-ended 'now', prevents a transaction still in flight from the external truth source from being mistaken for drift.

Introducing a CDC-driven path adds a new risk that the original full scan didn't have: a dropped or missed change event would silently hide real drift, so running a periodic full, unfiltered sweep alongside the activity-driven path (e.g. weekly) acts as a backstop that proves the filtered runs aren't missing anything.
This contract splits into three clear parts: observe, correct, and audit.

`snapshot` is the read-only operation — it compares each account's ledger balance against the external truth and returns per-account drift, writing nothing, so ops can call it as many times as they want with no side effect.

`run` is the mutating operation: it inserts a compensating `ledger_entry` for each drifted account, converges the balance back to the external truth, and returns a `runId`, a `driftCount`, and a `fixesApplied` list — each fix naming the account, ledger balance, truth balance, delta, direction, and compensating entry id, detailed enough to reconstruct exactly what happened without going back to the database.

`runs` is the audit query — run history newest-first, each row carrying the trigger (manual or scheduled), the drift count, and the status, so every correction can be traced back to the exact run that produced it.

The reason observation and correction must be separate: production almost never auto-fixes every drift — an unusually large drift is more often a sign of fraud than a bug — so ops needs to see the number first, then decide whether to alert, freeze the account, or apply a threshold that allows auto-fixing, and all of that must happen BEFORE anything mutates.

Separating the read path from the write path is what makes that decision safe: calling `snapshot` has no side effect, so polling it constantly carries no risk, while `run` is the one deliberate action allowed to write, so nobody accidentally triggers a correction just by wanting to check the current state.

Every money value (drift, ledgerBalance, truthBalance, delta) crosses the contract as a string rather than a number, to avoid losing precision once wallet balances exceed the safe range of a JSON numeric type, and so all four language implementations (TypeScript, Java, C#, Go) return exactly the same type for the same field.
A compensation that itself fails is the most dangerous case, and the design must guarantee it is never lost track of.

First, record the failure durably: when the credit-back call to wallet-service comes back with an error (say, wallet-service is down), the matching `saga_step` row flips to `failed` — never swallowed silently — so a recovery job can scan for and find it later.

Second, retry that compensation with exponential backoff; after N attempts still failing, route the step to a dead-letter queue and page on-call, instead of looping forever or quietly stopping — a human has to be pulled in once the automatic mechanism has run out of road.

Third, that retry must be idempotent: keyed by the pair `sagaId + step` so wallet-service can dedupe, which means no matter how many times the retry fires it can never double-credit the sender — the same mechanism class as guarding against double-debit on the forward step.

Fourth, any saga still stuck at `failed` past its retry budget needs to surface on a "stuck sagas" dashboard for ops, and depending on severity a wallet system may freeze the affected accounts until an operator resolves it manually — because an un-compensated saga means money is genuinely in an inconsistent state, not an incident that can just be ignored.

The whole design rests on one foundation: the `saga_step` table is the single source of truth, letting a recovery job (or an operator) always know exactly what happened and decide whether to continue or compensate next.
The goal is never "quietly move on" — the goal is always convergence: every saga eventually lands on `ok`, or gets resolved decisively by a human, never left hanging indefinitely.
The retried request has to be recognized as the same business transaction, and the only place that recognition can be guaranteed is the database.
Every transfer carries a `txnId`, and `ledger_entry` has a unique index on `(txnId, accountId, direction)`.
On the happy path, the service inserts the DEBIT/CREDIT pair for that `txnId` inside one Postgres transaction and commits.

When the client retries a request that already applied, the second attempt tries to insert that same pair again; the unique index rejects it, Postgres raises error `23505`, and the service catches that, rolls back, and returns `"replayed"` with both balances left untouched.
This holds under any concurrency or restart: two workers racing on the exact same `txnId` cannot both win the insert — the database serializes it so one gets the violation, full stop.

An in-memory or app-level pre-check, if it exists at all, is just a fast path to skip an obviously-duplicate request early; it is never what makes the guarantee true, because two workers can both read "not seen yet" from that check at the same instant.
The constraint being atomic with the write — not a separate step before or after it — is what actually makes exactly-once hold.
A failed forward step triggers its paired compensating step.

Here the debit succeeded and the credit failed, so the orchestrator issues a compensating credit-back on the sender — an ordinary credit call, this time targeting the sender's own wallet, that semantically reverses the earlier debit — and the saga reports "compensated" instead of "committed".
There is no special rollback RPC and no two-phase protocol involved: the compensation is just a forward business action run in reverse.
This is precisely why a saga can work across services that share nothing but an HTTP contract.
Because nothing is globally locked while the saga runs, a concurrent reader can briefly observe the sender already debited before the compensation lands and restores the balance.
So the system must be designed so that intermediate states are safe to observe, not treated as an impossible edge case.
None of this is guesswork for the orchestrator: the durable saga_step trail records each step's status (started, then ok or failed) before and after its HTTP call.
So at any point the orchestrator — or a recovery job, if it crashed — knows exactly what completed and what still needs to be undone.
Orchestration centralizes the flow in one place: payment-service owns the full sequence — calling debit, then credit, then running the compensation itself on failure

That centralization makes the saga a readable, linear state machine you can trace by opening one method, which is exactly why orchestration is easy to debug and reason about — but the price is that one component sits on the critical path of every transfer
Choreography removes the central driver: each service reacts to events on a broker and decides its own next action, so wallet-service and payment-service no longer call each other directly
That decoupling is what lets the design scale further, since no single component is coordinating every transfer

But the saga becomes implicit under choreography — its steps are scattered across many event handlers in different services instead of living in one method — so tracing a transfer means stitching together logs across services instead of reading one call stack

Compensation logic does not vanish in choreography — every 'X-done' event still needs a paired 'X-undone' handler, the same compensating-transaction discipline the orchestrator already has, just relocated
The pragmatic call is to start orchestrated, because clarity and debuggability matter most early and most wallet systems never actually hit the orchestrator's throughput ceiling
Move to choreography only when the single orchestrator is a measured bottleneck — not before, and not just because choreography sounds more 'modern' or scalable on paper
